description: We are Nebula X, a team of four united by our passion for education, technology, and the Universe. Our team includes two Pedagogy students, one Computer Science student, and an Agroecology Technology graduate collaborating from different cities. Together, we created Cosmic Archive, an interactive educational website that turns the stories of equipment left on the Moon and Mars into learning experiences, inspiring scientific curiosity in future generations.
summary:
Our team, NEBULOSA X, created Cosmic Archive, an educational and interactive website inspired by NASA’s challenge, “Abandoned but Not Forgotten.” The project invites children ages 8 to 14 to explore four pieces of equipment left on the Moon and Mars: the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, Surveyor 3, Opportunity, and Ingenuity.
Visitors choose a destination and discover how these technologies contributed to space exploration. On the Moon, they learn about Surveyor 3’s lunar soil tests and the Eagle descent stage, which remains at the Apollo 11 landing site. On Mars, they follow Opportunity’s search for evidence of past water and discover Ingenuity, designed for five flights but completing 72.
Through short stories, scientific facts, and interactive features, visitors explore the missions, track their progress in a travel journal, and test their knowledge with quizzes.
Our goal is to tell the story of space exploration through the equipment left behind, showing that every mission leaves a legacy. We aim to spark curiosity, encourage critical thinking, and connect new generations with science, education, and technology.
details:
On the website's first page, visitors will find a globe-shaped button accompanied by a short phrase inviting them to click and begin their space adventure.

The website is designed for children ages 8 to 14, with the aim of sparking curiosity about space and highlighting the importance of space missions to society. It supports the educational process and can be used as an educational resource or as a tool to reinforce learning, depending on the intended pedagogical objectives.

At this stage, children are invited to become astronauts through a playful, creative, and fun journey to discover the objects left behind during space missions that contributed to the advancement of humanity.

When visitors click on the planet, the website takes them to an introductory greeting, an explanation of the website's objectives, and the option to begin their journey. Children can choose their first destination. In this way, the website aims to introduce visitors to space artifacts that were used during important missions for humankind and left on the surfaces of Earth's natural satellite, the Moon, and the planet Mars after their respective missions came to an end.

At this point, a progress tab becomes available, allowing users to see which stage of the mission they have reached and track their progress. The website also features a travel journal where visitors can view their progress throughout their space journey. In this section, users can see completed objectives, overall progress, artifacts explored individually or by destination (the Moon or Mars), summaries of each artifact's discoveries, and an interesting fact about each one. The journal can also be closed. In this section, users can see which artifacts they have already explored and which ones are still locked.

Travelers are presented with two destination options: the Moon and Mars. They can choose which destination to visit and which stories about NASA's abandoned missions they would like to explore.

At this stage, visitors have two options. Under Destination 1, they can click on "Moon" and will be directed to another page where they can choose between two stories. The first is Apollo 11, which tells the story of the descent stage (Eagle), which remained on the Moon and was used to land the astronauts on the lunar surface. The second is Surveyor 3, the robotic spacecraft used to map the lunar surface before the first human mission to the Moon. To explore either story, visitors click on "Click to Investigate."

Visitors can also go back and choose Destination 2, the Red Planet, Mars. By clicking on "Mars," they will be directed to discover the stories of Ingenuity, which helped demonstrate that flight was possible on another planet and opened up new possibilities for space exploration, and Opportunity, which helped identify areas on the Martian surface showing signs of the presence of water.

To complete their exploration, young astronauts must answer a short quiz containing two questions about the artifact they have been investigating. The quiz appears as soon as they click on "Complete Story."

If they answer incorrectly, they have the option to select "Return to the Story" to revisit the artifact's story and answer the questions again at the end, or select "Continue Anyway," which will take them to the Moon exploration points. On this page, they can also select "Change Destination."

The quiz serves as a learning reinforcement tool and encourages users to test their knowledge of the stories presented.
